questions.q: Per ServiceNow Platform Development Lesson 1, who decides when an instance actually gets upgraded to a new platform release?
options: ServiceNow decides the release content and schedule; the customer decides when to apply the upgrade to their instance
ServiceNow applies every release to every customer instance automatically with no customer input
The customer controls what features are in each release
Upgrades only happen when a customer files a support ticket requesting one
questions.explain: ServiceNow owns the release calendar and content; the customer owns the decision and responsibility of when to upgrade their own instance.

questions.q: What does "systematic" pre-upgrade testing actually require, beyond casually clicking around the sandbox?
options: An actual inventory of every custom application, customization, and integration, tested deliberately against an upgraded sandbox
Testing only the applications the architect personally built
Waiting until production is upgraded and fixing issues as they're reported
Running the automated test framework once with no human review
questions.explain: Systematic testing means a real inventory of what exists on the instance, with each item deliberately validated — not spot-checking at random.

questions.q: A heavily-used scoped application relies on an API that ServiceNow is deprecating in the upcoming release. Where does this customization sit in upgrade triage, and why?
options: High-risk, high-usage tier — it gets thorough, hands-on validation first because of high blast radius and high likelihood of breaking
Low-risk tier — deprecated APIs are automatically handled by ServiceNow during upgrade
It doesn't need testing because it's a scoped application, not a global customization
It should be tested last since it's the most complex item
questions.explain: High usage plus a deprecated API dependency means high likelihood of breaking and high impact if it does — exactly the profile that goes first.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say enterprise upgrades often fail politically rather than technically?
options: Stakeholders finding out about the upgrade on upgrade day, with no advance notice, is often a bigger problem than a technical bug
Political failures and technical failures are the same thing in practice
Stakeholders never need to be informed about upgrades at all
Technical testing is unnecessary if stakeholders are informed early enough
questions.explain: A well-tested upgrade that still surprises application owners and business stakeholders is still a communication failure, even if nothing technical breaks.

questions.q: In the upgrade timeline this lesson describes, what should happen "months out" from the target upgrade window?
options: Communicate the target upgrade window to application owners and business stakeholders, not just IT
Perform the final go/no-go decision
Upgrade the production instance directly
Begin low-risk tier spot-checks only
questions.explain: Early, broad communication gives customization owners enough runway to test or request help — skipping this step is the most common upgrade-planning failure.
